findings.statement: CXCR2 tops the convergence ranking: pooled UC vs control log2FC is up [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.264], with an increase in all five cohorts and clinical-stage antagonists (reparixin, navarixin, ladarixin). In the same patients it is higher in inflamed than non-inflamed mucosa [gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=1.6972]. Caveat: CXCR2 is a neutrophil receptor, so the bulk rise most likely reflects neutrophil infiltration rather than a change in the epithelium (cell composition to be tested later).

The CXCR2 increase is mostly local to inflamed mucosa: non-inflamed MSCCR mucosa shows only a small rise versus control [gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=0.6399]. This makes it a marker of active local inflammation rather than a disease-wide lesion.

CXCL8 (IL-8), the ligand of CXCR1 and CXCR2, is strongly and reproducibly up (all five cohorts) [gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.7037], and is increased in inflamed vs non-inflamed mucosa of the same patient. Together with CXCR1, CXCR2 and CXCL1/CXCL5 it defines a coherent neutrophil-recruitment axis; bulk signal partly reflects infiltrating neutrophils and myeloid cells.

HMGCS2 (epithelial ketogenesis) is strongly lost in UC [gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.5845], decreased in all five cohorts, and lower in inflamed than non-inflamed mucosa of the same patient [gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=-1.9508]. Non-inflamed MSCCR mucosa is not different from control (padj [gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; padj=0.675]), so this is a local-inflammation biomarker of epithelial metabolic failure, not a likely drug target.

DUOX2 is among the largest and most reproducible increases (all five cohorts) [gene=DUOX2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.3213]. Unlike many genes it is also modestly raised in non-inflamed mucosa [gene=DUOX2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=0.8129], suggesting an epithelial change partly independent of overt inflammation; it has no approved drug.

OSMR (receptor of oncostatin M) is up in all five cohorts and has a genetic association in Open Targets; within patients it is higher in inflamed mucosa [gene=OSMR; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=0.8848]. The paired change is modest, so it is an inflammation-linked target candidate; stromal and immune cell origin must be checked.

JAK2 has the strongest genetic and tractability support among JAK genes but only a small expression change [gene=JAK2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=0.872], even though it is significant in all five cohorts. It is a pathway target (JAK-STAT) whose value does not come from a large transcript change.

CHI3L1 shows the largest reproducible increase among top-ranked genes (all five cohorts) [gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.7135], and is higher in inflamed than non-inflamed mucosa within patients. It is a candidate tissue marker of inflammation with no drug; contribution from macrophages and stroma cannot be excluded.

IDO1 is strongly induced in all five cohorts [gene=IDO1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.445] and is higher in inflamed mucosa within patients. It is an interferon-response gene (immune pathway), with IDO1 inhibitors existing in oncology; the signal likely comes from immune and epithelial cells responding to IFN-gamma.

CCL2 is raised in UC [gene=CCL2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.28], but data are present in only four cohorts (all four significant up), so replication is weaker than for CXCL8 or CXCR2, and the paired inflamed vs non-inflamed change is small. The anti-CCL2 antibody carlumab stopped at phase 2.

CLDN8 (epithelial tight junction) shows the largest pooled decrease [gene=CLDN8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-4.5181], decreasing in all five cohorts and in the paired inflamed contrast. Like other lost epithelial transport and metabolism genes (SLC26A2, PCK1, AQP8), it is a barrier/differentiation biomarker, not a target.

S100A8 (with S100A9, calprotectin) is strongly and reproducibly up in all five cohorts [gene=S100A8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.6467]. It is a neutrophil-derived signal, consistent with tissue-level support for faecal calprotectin as a biomarker, but it reflects cell infiltration rather than a tissue-intrinsic change.

caveats: Microarray fold changes are compressed relative to RNA-seq; only direction and significance were compared across cohorts.
Immune and neutrophil genes (CXCR1/2, CXCL8, S100A8/9, IDO1, CCL2) may be driven by infiltrating cells; cell-composition analysis is pending.
High heterogeneity (I2 mostly above 0.8) in pooled estimates: direction is consistent but effect size differs by cohort.
Some top genes (SLC6A14, DEFB4A, SAA2, TMIGD1) are measured in only two to four cohorts and were not prioritised.
Statements on paired and non-inflamed changes for CXCL8, CHI3L1, IDO1, CLDN8 and S100A8 come from the ranking summary; cited ids are the pooled records.
Expression alone does not establish causality or target safety.
